Here's my (limited) understanding. Bitcoin is supposed to be decentralised, meaning ideally there is no single party or concentration of power that needs to be trusted when using bitcoin. However at this time (or at least the time of the fork) the main computer code for bitcoin is developed by basically 5 main guys. Understandibly, these 5 guys are super hesitant to make big changes to the code because they don't want to break bitcoin. However changes must be made in order to advance bitcoin as usage and whatnot grows. This particular debate was mostly around the block size limit. Early on in bitcoin's development, the original creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, implemented an artificial limit on the block size. He did this so that a potential attacker on the Bitcoin network couldn't make a fake node with bad intent that would create a block that would be a massive size in order to hamper the network as a whole. However, since the blocks are where the transactions of the network are stored, this has the side effect of also limiting how many transactions the network can record. This state was fine while bitcoin was small but as usage grew, the number of transactions people were making was also growing and as of the time of the debate, the limit was starting to be hit.

Part of the reason the debate about this was so big was because people had different views of the consequences of the transaction limit being hit.

One group thought it was bad as the limit being hit would mean that people's transactions wouldn't make it into the next block and they would have to wait an average of 10 minutes for their transaction to be confirmed in the next block and since the last block was full, this block would most likely also be full so there could even be a running backlog of transactions not making it into the blocks. So people would start spamming the network with their transaction details, trying to get it into a block, having to increase the fees on transactions to get them to go through and whatnot all the while waiting in the real world unsure if when and if their transaction had gone through. Ultimately resulting in people giving up on bitcoin and generally being really bad for bitcoin's reputation and adoption.

Another group thought it wasn't so bad. After all the only reason miners mine bitcoin right now is to get the block rewards which is a small bit of new bitcoins that are created with each block, however this reward is set to slowly diminish as time moves on so eventually the only reason to run a full node and verify transactions will be to claim the fees from each transaction. This group thought having limited amounts of block confirmations would result in a better market for transaction fees. People would have to give higher fees to get their transactions included in the blockchain and therefore the miners would be rewarded for their "work".

A third group thought that bitcoin should stay small and not scale up at all because then it would be in danger of becoming too centralised.

This debate even took place among the 5 developers of bitcoin and they debated and debated of what solution was the best but they could not come to a unanimous decision about what to do. So in the spirit of bitcoin they took it to the community and let the comunity decide. Two of the developers forked the bitcoin core source code and made some changes to it, changes that would only become the rule if 75% of the last 1000 blocks mined, were mined by this version of the program, so that would basically mean that somewhere around 75% of the community was using the new forked version.

That's pretty much as much as I know. Since then i haven't heard too much about what the devs are doing but I know the forked version never really got high adoption from the community, I don't think it ever used by even 20% of the nodes on the network, However it's still around and could still be switched to by the community at any time if something happens to make them decide to switch. XTNodes.com has info about what's being run on the network at any given time.
